title.narrative: Emergency measures at Khortytsia National Reserve, in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine: documentation, digitization, and urgent conservation of threatened heritage sites and collection to enhance community resilience

description.narrative: Since the beginning of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine by the Russian Federation in February 2022, the war, in addition to the heavy human tool, has had a devastating impact on culture, heritage sites and cultural institutions, which are at the heart of community cohesion. Khortytsia National Reserve located in Zaporizhzhia oblast (south-east Ukraine) —the largest river island in Europe, and a site of exceptional natural and cultural heritage— has been heavily affected by the environmental fallout of the war. The area is continuously exposed to attacks, a situation that has been further aggravated in June 2023 due to the destruction of the closely situated Kakhovka Hydroelectric Power Plant. The area impacted by the dam destruction has a unique high-density concentration of cultural assets, several of which are of national importance, and includes, as revealed by the draining of the Kakhovka reservoir, an unprecedented number of archaeological sites and materials (ceramics, metal objects, flint tools, household items, and even a rare millennia-old oak log boat, etc.) that need urgent documentation and protection. These finds are of immense scientific and cultural importance, offering unique insights into prehistoric and medieval settlement of the region, but they are also at immediate risk of erosion, looting, and deterioration. Despite these obstacles, Khortytsia has continued to fulfil its broader mission as scientific and cultural institution, and resumed its role as a cultural hub, thus enhancing social resilience, through access to culture and continuity of cultural expressions and practices to foster communities’ ties, a sense of shared memory and identity and hope amid war. UNESCO has been supporting these efforts over the past two years, allowing researchers to survey some of the newly exposed areas of the riverbanks and incorporate over 2,000 newly identified artifacts into the Reserve’s collections. However, wartime conditions continue to threaten the Reserve, and its rich natural and cultural heritage, thus requiring the provided support to continue and be scaled up. The Project has the overall objective of providing a comprehensive response to war-induced damage while laying the foundation for sustainable preservation, knowledge exchange, and community engagement. In fact, the planned activities address both the very urgent and long-term needs of Khortytsia Reserve. Emergency measures, such as repairing the Museum premises, expanding storage facilities, and stabilizing rescued artifacts, are critical to prevent irreversible loss. Capacity-building initiatives —including paid apprenticeships, university partnerships, and specialized training— ensure that Khortytsia staff and a new generation of Ukrainian professionals gain advanced expertise in underwater archaeology and conservation, directly aligned with UNESCO’s best practices and conventions, particularly the 2001 Convention. Together, these activities provide a comprehensive response to war-induced damage while laying the foundation for sustainable preservation, knowledge exchange, and community engagement.
